WebFetch response caching is documented as 15 minutes per URL but in practice returned bodies from the 2026-09-02 run when this run requested the identical /api/feed URL strings 8 days later. Five feeds appeared frozen at their 09-01/09-02 content while the upstreams, fetched directly, were current to 09-09. Appending a per-run nonce query param to the dxedge URL (for example &nonce=0910a) changes the WebFetch cache key while leaving the backend behaviour identical, because /api/feed keys its own cache on the url param alone and FastAPI ignores the extra param. EVERY nightly /api/feed and /api/* check must carry a fresh nonce, or it is testing this container's cache instead of the site. A feed that looks stale should be confirmed against the upstream before it is reported. WORSE THAN DOCUMENTED, 2026-09-18: a CHANGED cache-busting param did not defeat it. /api/health?cb=20260918run1 at 04:14Z and /api/health?cb=20260918post at 05:00Z returned byte-identical bodies carrying the same 04:14:25Z timestamp, while a python fetch at 05:00Z returned a fresh 05:00:28Z. So a distinct cb/nonce value is necessary but NOT sufficient: WebFetch can still serve a cached body for a URL it has seen before with a different query string. Practical consequence: never judge post-deploy freshness from a WebFetch timestamp alone. Confirm it against a second, independent read of the same non-denied endpoint.

A TECHNIQUE, not a defect, and the most useful thing this run found. /api/debug lists the backend's live cache keys, and every proxied feed appears there as 'feedproxy:<exact upstream url>'. In backend/feedproxy.py fetch_feed, cache.set is reached ONLY on the HTTP 200 path: a non-200 raises FeedProxyError before it, a redirect with no Location raises, an over-cap body raises, and a disallowed host raises at validate() before any fetch happens. DEFAULT_TTL is 900s. Therefore the presence of a feedproxy key in /api/debug is proof that that exact feed returned 200 through the proxy within the last 15 minutes. One WebFetch of /api/debug thus answers, for EVERY feed on both standalone pages at once, the three questions Step 3 asks about non-200s, allowlist 403s and 502s. This matters because the Step 3 browser check can never run in a cloud scheduled session, and because it costs one request instead of seventeen, which also sidesteps api-rate-limit-on-feed. What it does NOT answer: whether a 200 body parsed correctly into its panel, whether the page logged a console error, and whether a panel is rendering an inline '<name> failed:' string. Those remain genuinely unchecked without a browser, and a run must say so rather than calling a cache-key sweep a render verdict.

So dxedge.net currently shows 116 on the dashboard and 92 on the cyber page, from the same origin, about 24 points apart. Security-relevant, pre-existing, and not previously tracked. frontend/src/components/Support.jsx renders the donation QR codes as pointing at a third party: https://api.qrserver.com/v1/create-qr-code/?size=NxN&data=&bgcolor=0e0e0e&color=7affb2&qzone=2. The values passed in the data param are the page's BTC address (bc1q99...dgxl), ETH address (0x450Af...82db), https://paypal.me/sagejw and now https://ko-fi.com/oldtimeradio. CONCRETE RISK, and it is worse than the ordinary third-party-asset case: the QR is the artifact a visitor actually scans, and a compromised, hijacked or MITM'd api.qrserver.com could return a QR encoding a DIFFERENT wallet address while the plain-text address printed next to it stays correct. People scan QR codes without reading the address underneath, so donations would silently redirect with no visible tell and no integrity check available - an cannot carry subresource integrity, and the URL is built fresh on every render. Secondary issues: the addresses are disclosed to a third party on every page view (minor, they are public by design), and the QRs break if the service goes down. PROVENANCE, stated precisely so this is not misread as a regression: Support.jsx was added by James himself in 59111ba on 2026-05-31, and the 7 OTR commits of 2026-10-01 only changed its KOFI constant. The dependency is James's own and about four months old. It surfaced tonight only because reviewing those commits meant reading the file, and it appears in neither known_issues nor awaiting_james, so it has never been reported. NOT fixed autonomously: it is not link rot, not a redirect, not a deprecated feed endpoint and not an /api/feed bypass (an image load is not a CORS fetch and cannot go through a proxy that returns text, same reasoning as otr-audio-is-a-media-element-not-a-feed), so it falls outside all four repair categories. It is also closely analogous to crane-cab-third-party-cdn, which was escalated rather than fixed. OPTIONS: (a) leave as is; (b) generate the QR codes client-side from a vendored QR library, which removes the third party entirely and is the clean fix; (c) pre-generate the four QR PNGs once, eyeball-verify each decodes to the right address, and commit them as static assets, which also removes the runtime dependency and is the smallest change; (d) drop the QR codes and show copy-to-clipboard text addresses only. Recommend (c) for the crypto addresses specifically, since those are the ones where a swap costs real money and the address set almost never changes. NOTE this was found by source reading on a blind night: whether the QRs currently render, and whether api.qrserver.com is even reachable, was NOT verified.
